LSJ / STEPBible (TFLSJ)
Related to:  εἰ,
Attic dialect-Ionic dialect and [Refs 4th c.AD+ [4th c.AD(?): Arcadius Grammaticus (for εἰκ, see below 11 ad [near the start]), = _Doric dialect_ and _Aeolic dialect_ αἰ, αἰκ (which see), 5th c.AD: Cypria]] ἤ [Refs [“Inscription Cyprian dialect” 135.10 H., both εἰ and αἰ]] in Epic dialect:— Particle used interjectionally with imperative and to express a wish, but usually either in conditions, if, or in indirect questions, whether. In the former use its regular negative is μ; in the latter, οὐ.

__A
INTERJECTIONALLY, in [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus]], come now! with imperative, εἰ δὲ.. ἄκουσον [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 9.262; εἰ δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ φευγόντων [prev. work] 46; most frequently with ἄγε (which see), 1.302, +others]]

__A.2
in wishes, with optative, ἀλλ᾽ εἴ τις.. καλέσειεν [Refs [10.111, compare 24.74]]; so later, εἴ μοι ξυνείη μοῖρα [Refs 8th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Tyrannus” 863 (Lyric poetry); εἴ μοι γένοιτο φθόγγος ἐν βραχίοσιν 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Hecuba” 836: more frequently followed by γάρ, αἲ γὰρ δὴ οὕτως εἴη 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 4.189, +others; εἰ γὰρ γενοίμην ἀντὶ σοῦ νεκρός 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Hippolytus” 1410; εἰ γὰρ γένοιτο 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 6.1.38; εἰ γὰρ ἐν τούτῳ εἴη 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Protagoras” 310d]]; of unattained wishes, in [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus only with _optative_, εἰ γὰρ ἐγὼν.. Διὸς πάϊς αἰγιόχοιο εἴην 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 13.825; Ζεῦ πάτερ, αἰ γὰρ ἐμὸς πόσις εἴη 7th c.BC: Alcman Lyricus 29]]; later with past tenses of indicative, εἰ γάρ μ᾽ ὑπὸ γῆν.. ἧκεν [Refs 4th c.BC+ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Prometheus Vinctus” 152 (_anapaest meter_)]]; εἰ γὰρ τοσαύτην δύναμιν εἶχον ὥστε.. [Refs 8th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Alcestis” 1072: twice in 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” with]]infinitive (compare the use of infinitive in commands), αἰ γὰρ τοῖος ἐὼν.. ἐμὸς γαμβρὸς καλέεσθαι [Refs [7.311, compare 24.376.]]

__A.2.b
εἴθε, Epic dialect αἴθε, is frequently used in wishes in the above constructions, εἴθε οἱ αὐτῷ Ζεὺς ἀγαθὸν τελέσειεν [Refs 8th c.BC+ [2.33; εἴθ᾽ ὣς ἡβώοιμι 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 7.157; ἰὼ γᾶ, εἴθ᾽ ἔμ᾽ ἐδέξω 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Agamemnon” 1537 (Lyric poetry); εἴθε σοι, ὦ Περίκλεις, τότε συνεγενόμην 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Memorabilia” 1.2.46]]: later with infinitive, γαίης χθαμαλωτέρη εἴθε.. κεῖσθαι [Refs 1st c.BC+ [“Anthologia Graeca” 9.284 (1st c.BC-1st c.AD: Crinagoras Epigrammaticus).]]

__A.2.c
εἰ γάρ, εἴθε are also used with ὤφελον (Epic dialect ὤφελλον), of past unattained wishes, αἴθ᾽ ὤφελλες στρατοῦ ἄλλου σημαίνειν [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 14.84]]; εἰ γὰρ ὤφελον [κατιδεῖν] [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 432c.]]

__A.2.d
followed by a clause expressing a consequence of the fulfilment of the wish, αἰ γὰρ τοῦτο.. ἔπος τετελεσμένον εἴη· τῷ κε τάχα γνοίης.. [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 15.536, compare 17.496, +others]]; sometimes hard to distinguish from εἰ in conditions (which may be derived from this use), εἴ μοί τι πίθοιο, τό κεν πολὺ κέρδιον εἴη [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 7.28.]]

__B
IN CONDITIONS, if:

__B.I
with INDIC.,

__B.I.1
with all tenses (for future, see below [Refs [2), to state a condition, with nothing implied as to its fulfilment, εἰ δ᾽ οὕτω τοῦτ᾽ ἐστίν, ἐμοὶ μέλλει φίλον εἶναι but]]if this is so, it will be.., [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.564]]: any form of the Verb may stand in apodosi, εἰ θεοί τι δρῶσιν αἰσχρόν, οὐκ εἰσὶν θεοί [Refs 8th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Fragmenta” 292.7; εἰ δοκεῖ, πλέωμεν 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 526; εἰ Φαῖδρον ἀγνοῶ, καὶ ἐμαυτοῦ ἐπιλέλησμαι 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedrus” 228a; κάκιστ᾽ ἀπολοίμην, Ξανθίαν εἰ μὴ φιλῶ 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Ranae” 579, compare 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 17.475; εἰ θεοῦ ἦν, οὐκ ἦν αἰσχροκερδής· εἰ δ᾽ αἰσχροκερδής, οὐκ ἦν θεοῦ 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 408c; εἰ ταῦτα λέγων διαφθείρω τοὺς νέους, ταῦτ᾽ ἂν εἴη βλαβερά [prev. author] “Ap.” 30b, compare 25b]]; εἰ οὗτοι ὀρθῶς ἀπέστησαν, ὑμεῖς ἂν οὐ χρεὼν ἄρχοιτε if these were right in their revolt, (it would follow that) you rule when you have no right, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 3.40.]]

__B.I.1.b
to express a general condition, if ever, whenever, sometimes with present, εἴ τις δύο ἢ καὶ πλείους τις ἡμέρας λογίζεται, μάταιός ἐστιν [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Trachiniae” 943]]: with imperfect, εἴ τίς τι ἠρώτα ἀπεκρίνοντο [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 7.10]]: rarely with aorist, [Refs 1st c.BC+ [1st c.BC: Diodorus Siculus Historicus 31.26.1, 2nd c.AD: Sextus Empiricus Philosophus “Πυρρώνειοι ὑποτυπώσεις” 1.84; compare 111.2.]]

__B.I.2
with future (much less frequently than ἐάν with subjunctive), either to express a future supposition emphatically, εἰ φθάσομεν τοὺς πολεμίους κατακαίνοντες οὐδεὶς ἡμῶν ἀποθανεῖται [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 7.1.19; εἰ μὴ βοηθήσετε οὐ περιέσται τἀκεῖ 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 6.91; εἰ αὕτη ἡ πόλις ληφθήσεται, ἔχεται ἡ πᾶσα Σικελία [prev. passage];]] in threats or warnings, εἰ μὴ καθέξεις γλῶσσαν ἔσται σοι κακά [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Fragmenta” 5; εἰ τιμωρήσεις Πατρόκλῳ, αὐτὸς ἀποθανῇ 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Apologia” 28c, compare 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 28.21: or,]]

__B.I.2.b
to express a present intention or expectation, αἶρε πλῆκτρον εἰ μαχεῖ if you mean to fight, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Aves” 759; ἐγὼ μὲν οὐκ ἀνήρ.. εἰ ταῦτ᾽ ἀνατεὶ τῇδε κείσεται κράτη 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Antigone” 485, compare 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.61, 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Hecuba” 863.]]

__B.I.3
with historical tenses, implying that the condition is or was unfulfilled.

__B.I.3.a
with imperfect, referring to present time or to continued or repeated action in past time (in [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus always the latter, 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 24.715, +others): ταῦτα οὐκ ἂν ἐδύναντο ποιεῖν, εἰ μὴ διαίτῃ μετρίᾳ ἐχρῶντο they would not be able to do this (as they do)]], if they did not live an abstemious life, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 1.2.16, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 489b; οὐκ ἂν νήσων ἐκράτει, εἰ μή τι καὶ ναυτικὸν εἶχεν he (from Agamemnon)]] would not have been master of islands, if he had not had also some naval force, [Refs 7th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.9; αἰ δ᾽ ἦχες ἔσλων ἴμερον ἢ κάλων.. αἴδως κεν.. ἦχεν 7th-6th c.BC: Sappho Lyrica 28]]; εἰ ἦσαν ἄνδρες ἀγαθοὶ.. οὐκ ἄν ποτε ταῦτα ἔπασχον if they had been good men, they would never have suffered as they did, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Gorgias” 516e, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Memorabilia” 1.1.5]]; εἰ γὰρ ἐγὼ τάδε ᾔδἐ.. οὐκ ἂν ὑπεξέφυγε if I had known this.., [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 8.366.]]

__B.I.3.b
with aorist referring to past time, εἰ μὴ ἔφυσε θεὸς μέλι.. ἔφασκον γλύσσονα σῦκα πέλεσθαι [Refs 6th c.BC+ [6th c.BC: Xenophanes Poeta Philosophus 38]]; εἰ μὴ ὑμεῖς ἤλθετε, ἐπορευόμεθα ἂν ἐπὶ βασιλέα had you not come, we should be on our way.., [Refs 8th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 2.1.4; καὶ ἴσως ἂν ἀπέθανον, εἰ μὴ ἡ ἀρχὴ διὰ ταχέων κατελύθη 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Apologia” 32d, compare 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 5.680, 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 4.364, 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 4.5, 27.63]]: with pluperfect in apodosi, εἰ τριάκοντα μόναι μετέπεσον τῶν ψήφων, ἀπεπεφεύγη ἄν [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Apologia” 36a.]]

__B.I.3.c
rarely with pluperfect referring to action finished in past or present time, λοιπὸν δ᾽ ἂν ἦν ἡμῖν ἔτι περὶ τῆς πόλεως διαλεχθῆναι, εἰ μὴ προτέρα τῶν ἄλλων τὴν εἰρήνην ἐπεποίητο if she had not (as she has done) made peace before the rest, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Isocrates Orator 5.56, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Timaeus” 21c.]]

__B.II
with SUB[Refs 1st c.AD+ [1st c.AD: Josephus Historicus, εἰ is regularly joined with ἄν]] (Epic dialect κε, κεν), compare ἐάν: [Refs 4th c.BC+ [4th c.AD(?): Arcadius Grammaticus εἰκαν in Tegean Inscrr. of 4th c.BC (“IG” 5(2).3.16, 31, 6.2, “SIG” 306.34) should be understood as εἰκ ἄν (εἰ: εἰκ ={οὐ}: οὐκ), since εἰ δ᾽ ἄν is also found in “IG” 5(2).3.2, 6.45, and εἰκ alone, [prev. work]3.21]]; but ἄν (κε, κεν) are frequently absent in [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus as 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 5.221, 14.373 (and compare below 2), and Lyric poetry, 5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus (who never uses εἰ with ἄν or κε (ν)) “P.” 4.266, +others; in dialects, αἰ δείλητ᾽ ἀγχωρεῖν “IG” 9(1).334.6 (_Locrian dialect_, 5th c.BC)]], cf. Foed.Doric dialect cited in [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 5.79; rarely in 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus, εἰ μὴ ἀναβῇ 2.13]]; occasionally in Trag., [Refs 5th c.BC+ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Eumenides” 234, 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Tyrannus” 198 (Lyric poetry), etc.]]; very rarely in Attic dialect Prose, εἰ ξυστῶσιν αἱ πόλεις [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 6.21; εἴ τι που ἄλσος ἢ τέμενος ἀφειμένον ᾖ 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Leges” 761c]]: in later Prose, εἴ τις θελήσῃ [NT+3rd c.AD+ [NT.Rev.11.5; εἰ φονεύῃ 3rd c.AD: Plotinus Philosophus 2.9.9, compare 5th c.AD: Proclus Philosophus “Inst.” 26.]]

__B.II.1
when the apodosis is future, to express a future condition more distinctly and vividly than εἰ with optative, but less so than εἰ with future indicative (above [Refs [1.2a)]]; εἰ δέ κεν ὣς ἕρξῃς καί τοι πείθωνται Ἀχαιοί, γνώσῃ ἔπειθ᾽.. if thou do thus.., thou shalt know, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 2.364, compare 1.128, 3.281, 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 17.549; ἂν δέ τις ἀνθιστῆται, σὺν ὑμῖν πειρασόμεθα χειροῦσθαι 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 7.3.11]]; ἂν μὴ νῦν ἐθέλωμεν ἐκεῖ πολεμεῖν αὐτῷ, ἐνθάδ᾽ ἴσως ἀναγκασθησόμεθα τοῦτο ποιεῖν if we be not now willing, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 4.50, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 5.3.27: followed by _imperative_, ἢν εἰρήνης δοκῆτε δεῖσθαι, ἄνευ ὅπλων ἥκετε [prev. work] 3.2.13, compare 5.4.30.]]

__B.II.2
when the apodosis is present, denoting customary or repeated action, to express a general condition, if ever, ἤν ποτε δασμὸς ἵκηται, σοὶ τὸ γέρας πολὺ μεῖζον (i.e. ἐστί) whenever a division comes, your prize is (always) greater, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.166]]; ἢν ἐγγὺς ἔλθῃ θάνατος, οὐδεὶς βούλεται θνῄσκειν if death come near, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Alcestis” 671]]; with ἄν omitted, εἴ περ γάρ τε χόλον.. καταπέψῃ ἀλλά.. ἔχει κότον [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.81.]]

__B.II.2.b
with Rhet. present in apodosis, ἐὰν μὴ οἱ φιλόσοφοι βασιλεύσωσιν, οὐκ ἔστι κακῶν παῦλα there is (i.e. can be, will be) no rest.., [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 473d.]]

__B.III
with OPTATIVE (never with ἄν in early Gr., later ἐάν with optative, [Refs 5th c.AD+ [5th-6th c.AD: Damascius Philosophus “de Principiis” 114, +others),]]

__B.III.1
to express a future condition less definitely than ἐάν with subjunctive, usually with optative with ἄν in apodosis, ἦ κεν γηθήσαι Πρίαμος Πριάμοιό τε παῖδες.. εἰ σφῶιν τάδε πάντα πυθοίατο μαρναμένοιιν surely they would exult, if they should hear.., [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.255, compare 7.28, 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 3.223; εἴης φορητὸς οὐκ ἄν, εἰ πράσσοις καλῶς 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Prometheus Vinctus” 979; οὐδὲ γὰρ ἄν με ἐπαινοίη, εἰ ἐξελαύνοιμι τοὺς εὐεργέτας 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 7.7.11; οἶκος δ᾽ αὐτός, εἰ φθογγὴν λάβοι, σαφέστατ᾽ ἂν λέξειεν 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Agamemnon” 37, etc.]]: future optative is falsa lectio in [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Theaetetus” 164a]]: with present indicative in apodosis, [Refs 6th c.BC+ [6th c.BC: Xenophanes Poeta Philosophus 34.3, 3rd c.AD: Democritus Epigrammaticus 253]]: with future indicative, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Melissus Philosophus 5.]]

__B.III.1.b
in Hom.sometimes with present optative, to express an unfulfilled present condition, εἰ μὲν νῦν ἐπὶ ἄλλῳ ἀεθλεύοιμεν, ἦ τ᾽ ἂν ἐγὼ τὰ πρῶτα φεροίμην if we were now contending, etc., [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 23.274: rarely in Trag., εἰ μὴ κνίζοι (={εἰ μὴ ἔκνιζε}) 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Medea” 568; also εἰ ἀναγκαῖον εἴη ἀδικεῖν ἢ ἀδικεῖσθαι, ἑλοίμην ἂν μᾶλλον ἀδικεῖσθαι 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Gorgias” 469c.]]

__B.III.2
when the apodosis is past, denoting customary or repeated action, to express a general condition in past time (corresponding to use of subjunctive in present time, above [Refs [11.2)]]; once in [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus, εἴ τίς με.. ἐνίπτοι, ἀλλὰ σὺ τόν γ᾽.. κατέρυκες 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 24.768]]; εἰ δέ τινας θορυβουμένους αἴσθοιτο.., κατασβεννύναι τὴν ταραχὴν ἐπειρᾶτο if he should see (whenever he saw) any troops in confusion, he (always) tried, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 5.3.55, compare “An.” 4.5.13, “Mem.” 4.2.40]]; εἴ τις ἀντείποι, εὐθὺς ἐτεθνήκει if any one made objection, he was a dead man at once, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 8.66; ἀλλ᾽ εἴ τι μὴ φέροιμεν, ὤτρυνεν φέρειν 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Alcestis” 755. For εἰ with _indicative_ in this sense see above 1.1]]: indicative and optative are found in same sentence, ἐμίσει, οὐκ εἴ τις κακῶς πάσχων ἠμύνετο, ἀλλ᾽ εἴ τις εὐεργετούμενος ἀχάριστος φαίνοιτο [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Agesilaus” 11.3.]]

__B.III.3
in oratio obliqua after past tenses, representing ἐάν with subjunctive or εἰ with a primary (never an historical) tense of the indicative in oratio recta, ἐλογίζοντο ὡς, εἰ μὴ μάχοιντο, ἀποστήσοιντο αἱ πόλεις (representing ἐὰν μὴ μαχώμεθα, ἀποστήσονται) [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Historia Graeca (Hellenica)” 6.4.6, compare 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 21.104, 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Historia Graeca (Hellenica)” 5.2.2]]; ἔλεγεν ὅτι, εἰ βλαβερὰ πεπραχὼς εἴη, δίκαιος εἴη ζημιοῦσθαι (representing εἰ βλαβερὰ πέπραχε, δίκαιός ἐστι)[Refs [[prev. work] 32, compare “An.” 6.6.25]]; εἰ δέ τινα φεύγοντα λήψοιτο, προηγόρευεν ὅτι ὡς πολεμίῳ χρήσοιτο (representing εἴ τινα λήψομαι, χρήσομαι) [Refs [[prev. author] “Cyr.” 3.1.3]]; also, where oratio obliqua is implied in the leading clause, οὐκ ἦν τοῦ πολέμου πέρας Φιλίππῳ, εἰ μὴ Θηβαίους.. ἐχθροὺς ποιήσειε τῇ πόλει, i.e. Philip thought there would be no end to the war, unless he should make.. (his thought having been ἐὰν μὴ ποιήσω), [Refs 5th c.BC+ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 18.145; ἐβούλοντο γὰρ σφίσιν, εἴ τινα λάβοιεν, ὑπάρχειν ἀντὶ τῶν ἔνδον, ἢν ἄρα τύχωσί τινες ἐζωγρημένοι 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 2.5.]]

__B.III.4
with optative with ἄν, only when the clause serves as apodosis as well as protasis,[Refs 5th c.BC+ [compare 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Protagoras” 329b, 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 4.18, 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Memorabilia” 1.5.3 (see. ἄν 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus 111. d).]]

__B.IV
with infinitive, in oratio obliqua, only in [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus, εἰ γὰρ δὴ δεῖν πάντως περιθεῖναι ἄλλῳ τέῳ τὴν βασιληΐην, [ἔφη] δικαιότερον εἶναι κτλ. 1.129; εἰ εἶναι τοῦτο μὴ φίλον 2.64, compare 172, 3.105, 108.]]

__B.V
after Verbs denoting wonder, delight, indignation, disappointment, contentment, and similar emotions, εἰ with indicative is used instead of ὅτι, to express the object of the feeling in a hypothetical form, θαυμάζω εἰ μηδεὶς ὑμῶν μήτ᾽ ἐνθυμεῖται μήτ᾽ ὀργίζεται, ὁρῶν.. I wonder that no one of you is either concerned or angry when he sees.., [Refs 4th c.BC+ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 4.43; οὐκ ἀγαπᾷ εἰ μὴ δίκην δέδωκεν, ἀλλ᾽ εἰ μὴ καὶ χρυσῷ στεφάνῳ στεφανωθήσεται ἀγανακτεῖ 4th c.BC: Aeschines Orator 3.147]]: after past tenses, ἐθαύμασε δ᾽ εἰ μὴ φανερόν ἐστιν [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Memorabilia” 1.1.13; δεινὸν εἰσῄει, εἰ μὴ.. δόξει 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 19.33; ἐθαύμαζον εἴ τι ἕξει τις χρήσασθαι τῷ λόγῳ 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedo” 95a; οὐδὲ ᾐσχύνθη εἰ.. ἐπάγει 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 21.105: in oratio obliqua (expressed or implied) with _optative_, ἐπεῖπεν ὡς δεινὸν (i.e. εἴη) εἰ.. μεγαλόψυχος γένοιτο 4th c.BC: Aeschines Orator 2.157; ᾤκτιρον εἰ ἁλώσοιντο 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 1.4.7]]; ἐθαύμαζε δ᾽ εἴ τις ἀρετὴν ἐπαγγελλόμενος ἀργύριον πράττοιτο he wondered that any one should demand money, [Refs [[prev. author] “Mem.” 1.2.7]]; ἔχαιρον ἀγαπῶν εἴ τις ἐάσοι I rejoiced, being content if any one should let it pass, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 450a:]] —in this use the _negative_ οὐ is also found, ἀγανακτῶ εἰ ὁ Φίλιππος ἁρπάζων οὐ λυπεῖ [Refs 5th c.BC+ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 8.55; δεινὸν ἂν εἴη εἰ οἱ ἐκείνων ξύμμαχοι οὐκ ἀπεροῦσιν 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.121; τέρας λέγεις, εἰ οὐκ ἂν δύναιντο λαθεῖν 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Meno” 91d, etc.]]

__B.VI
in citing a fact as a ground of argument or appeal, as surely as, since, εἴ ποτ᾽ ἔην γε if there was [as there was], i.e. as sure as there was such an one, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 3.180, +others; εἰ τότε κοῦρος ἔα, νῦν αὖτέ με γῆρας ὀπάζει 4.321]]; πολλοὺς γὰρ οἶκε εἶναι εὐπετέστερον διαβάλλειν ἢ ἕνα, εἰ Κλεομένεα μὲν μοῦνον οὐκ οἷός τε ἐγένετο διαβαλεῖν, τρεῖς δὲ μυριάδας Ἀθηναίων ἐποίησε τοῦτο it seems easier to deceive many than one, if (as was the fact, i.e. since) he was not able.., [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 5.97, compare 1.60, +others]]

__B.VII
ELLIPTICAL CONSTRUCTIONS:

__B.VII.1
with apodosis implied in the context, εἰ having the force of in case, supposing that, πρὸς τὴν πόλιν, εἰ ἐπιβοηθοῖεν, ἐχώρουν they marched towards the city [so as to meet the citizens], in case they should rush out, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 6.100]]; ἱκέται πρὸς σὲ δεῦρ᾽ ἀφίγμεθα, εἴ τινα πόλιν φράσειας ἡμῖν εὔερον we have come hither to you, in case you should tell us of some fleecy city (i.e. that we might hear of it), [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Aves” 120]]; παρέζεο καὶ λαβὲ γούνων, αἴ κέν πως ἐθέλῃσιν ἐπὶ Τρώεσσιν ἀρῆξαι sit by him and grasp his knees [so as to persuade him], in case he be willing to help the Trojans, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.408, compare 66, 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 1.94, 3.92]]; ἄκουσον καὶ ἐμοῦ, ἐάν σοι ἔτι ταὐτὰ δοκῇ hear me also [that you may assent], in case the same opinion please you, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 358b]]; ἰδὲ δή, ἐάν σοι ὅπερ ἐμοὶ συνδοκῇ look now, in case you approve what I do, [Refs [[prev. work] 434a.]]

__B.VII.2
with apodosis suppressed for rhetorical reasons, εἴ περ γάρ κ᾽ ἐθέλῃσιν Ὀλύμπιος.. στυφελίξαι if he wish to thrust him away, [he will do so], [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.580]]; εἰ μὲν δώσουσι γέρας—· εἰ δέ κε μὴ δώωσιν, ἐγὼ δέ κεν αὐτὸς ἕλωμαι if they shall give me a prize, [well and good]; but if they give not, then I will take one for myself, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [1.135, compare 6.150, 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Plutus” 468]]; καὶ ἢν μὲν ξυμβῇ ἡ πεῖρα—· εἰ δὲ μή.. and if the attempt succeed, [well]; otherwise.., [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 3.3, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Protagoras” 325d.]]

__B.VII.3
with the Verb of the protasis omitted, chiefly in the following expressions:

__B.VII.3.a
εἰ μή except, οὐδὲν ἄλλο σιτέονται, εἰ μὴ ἰχθῦς μοῦνον [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.200]]; μὰ τὼ θεώ, εἰ μὴ Κρίτυλλά γ᾽ [εἰμί]—nay, if I'm not Critylla! i.e. I am, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Thesmophoriazusae” 898]]; εἰ μὴ ὅσον except only, ἐγὼ μέν μιν οὐκ εἶδον, εἰ μὴ ὅσον γραφῇ [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 2.73, compare 1.45, 2.20; εἰ μὴ εἰ 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.17, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Gorgias” 480b, etc.]]; εἰ μή τι οὖν, ἀλλὰ σμικρόν γέ μοι τῆς ἀρχῆς χάλασον if nothing else, yet.., [Refs 5th c.BC+ [[prev. author] “Men.” 86e; ironical, εἰ μὴ ἄρα ἡ τῆς ἀρετῆς ἐπιμέλεια διαφθορά ἐστιν 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Memorabilia” 1.2.8; εἰ μή πέρ γε τὸν ὑοσκύαμον χρήματα εἶναι φήσομεν [prev. author] “Oec.” 1.13.]]

__B.VII.3.b
εἰ δὲ μή but if not, i.e. otherwise, προηγόρευε τοῖς Λαμψακηνοῖσι μετιέναι Μιλτιάδεα, εἰ δὲ μή, σφέας πίτυος τρόπον ἀπείλεε ἐκτρίψειν [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 6.37, compare 56]]; after μάλιστα μέν, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.32, 35, etc.:]] —after a preceding _negative_, μὴ τύπτ᾽· εἰ δὲ μή, σαυτόν ποτ᾽ αἰτιάσει don't beat me; otherwise, you will have yourself to blame, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Nubes” 1433; ὦ Κῦρε, μὴ οὕτω λέγε· εἰ δὲ μή, οὐ θαρροῦντά με ἕξεις 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 3.1.35; οὔτ᾽ ἐν τῷ ὕδατι τὰ ὅπλα ἦν ἔχειν· εἰ δὲ μή [prev. author] “An.” 4.3.6, compare 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.28, 131, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedo” 91c.]]

__B.VII.3.c
εἰ δέ sometimes stands for εἰ δὲ μή, εἰ μὲν βούλεται, ἑψέτω· εἰ δ᾽, ὅτι βούλεται, τοῦτο ποιείτω [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Euthydemus” 285c, compare “Smp.” 212c; εἰ δ᾽ οὖν 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Antigone” 722; εἰ δ᾽ οὕτως 4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “Ethica Nicomachea” 1094a24]]; εἰ δὲ τοῦτο and if so, [Refs 1st c.BC+ [1st c.BC-1st c.AD: Strabo Geographus 2.1.29.]]

__B.VII.3.d
εἰ γάρ for if so, [Refs [[prev. author] 7.3.6.]]

__B.VII.3.e
εἴ τις if any, i. e. as much as or more than any, τῶν γε νῦν αἴ τις ἐπιχθονίων, ὀρθῶς [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Bacchylides Lyricus 5.5; ὄτλον ἄλγιστον ἔσχον, εἴ τις Αἰτωλὶς γυνή 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Trachiniae” 8, compare “OC” 734]]; εἴ τις ἄλλος, siquis alius, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Andromache” 6, etc.; εἴ τινες καὶ ἄλλοι 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 3.2, etc.; εἴπερ τις ἄλλος 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 501d]]; also κατ᾽ εἰ δέ τινα τρόπον in any way, [Refs [“IG” 5(2).6.27 (from Tegea).]]

__B.VII.3.f
εἴ ποτε or εἴπερ ποτέ now if ever, ἡμῖν δὲ καλῶς, εἴπερ ποτέ, ἔχει.. ἡ ξυναλλαγή [Refs 7th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 4.20, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Equites” 594; αἴ ποτα κἄλλοτα 7th-6th c.BC: Alcaeus Lyricus “Supp.” 7.11, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 6.4.12, etc.]]; but in prayers, εἴ ποτέ τοι ἐπὶ νηὸν ἔρεψα.. τόδε μοι κρήηνον ἐέλδωρ [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.39.]]

__B.VII.3.g
εἴ ποθεν (i.e. δυνατόν ἐστι) if from any quarter, i.e. from some quarter or other, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 1204 (Lyric poetry)]]; so εἴ ποθι somewhere, anywhere, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [[prev. author] “Aj.” 885 (Lyric poetry); εἴ που 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 4.193.]]

__B.VII.3.h
εἴ πως[Refs 5th c.BC+ [[prev. work] 388, 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 2.3.11]]: in an elliptical sentence (cf. VII. [Refs 5th c.BC+ [1), πρέσβεις πέμψαντες, εἴ πως πείσειαν 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.58.]]

__B.VIII
with other PARTICLES:

__B.VIII.1
for the distinction between καὶ εἰ (or καὶ ἐάν, or κἄν) even if, and εἰ καί (or ἐὰν καί) even though, see at {καί}:—the opposite of καὶ εἰ is οὐδ᾽ εἰ, not even if; that of εἰ καί is εἰ μηδέ, if (although) not even.

__B.VIII.2
for ὡς εἰ, ὡς εἴ τε, ὥσπερ εἰ, etc., see at {ὡς} and ὥσπερ.

__B.VIII.3
for εἰ ἄρα, see at {ἄρα}; for εἰ δή, εἴπερ, see at {εἰ δή, εἴπερ}; for εἴ γε, see at {γέ}.

__B.IX
in negative oaths, = Hebrew im, [LXX+NT [LXX.Psa.94(95).11, NT.Mark.8.12, +others]]

__C
IN INDIRECT QUESTIONS, whether, followed by the indicative, subjunctive, or optative, according to the principles of oratio obliqua:

__C.1
with IN[Refs 4th c.BC+ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator after primary tenses, representing the same tense in the direct question, σάφα δ᾽ οὐκ οἶδ᾽ εἰ θεός ἐστιν]] whether he is a god, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 5.183; εἰ ξυμπονήσεις.. σκόπει 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Antigone” 41.]]

__C.2
with SUB[Refs 1st c.AD+ [1st c.AD: Josephus Historicus after primary tenses, representing a dubitative]]subjunctive in the direct question, τὰ ἐκπώματα οὐκ οἶδ᾽ εἰ Χρυσάντᾳ τουτῳῒ δῶ whether I should give them, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 8.4.16: sometimes elliptical, ἐς τὰ χρηστήρια ἔπεμπε, εἰ στρατεύηται ἐπὶ τοὺς Πέρσας 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.75.]]

__C.3
OPT. after past tenses, representing either of the two previous constructions in the direct question, ἤρετο εἴ τις ἐμοῦ εἴη σοφώτερος he asked whether any one was wiser than I (direct ἔστι τις σοφώτερο;), [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Apologia” 21a; ἐπεκηρυκεύετο Πεισιστράτῳ, εἰ βούλοιτό οἱ τὴν θυγατέρα ἔχειν γυναῖκα 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.60: rarely]]aorist optative for the aorist indicative, ἠρώτων αὐτὸν εἰ ἀναπλεύσειεν I asked him whether he had set sail (direct ἀνέπλευσα;), [Refs 4th c.BC+ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 50.55: but]]aorist optative usually represents aorist subjunctive, τὸν θεὸν ἐπήροντο εἰ παραδοῖεν Κορινθίοις τὴν πόλιν.. καὶ τιμωρίαν τινὰ πειρῷντ᾽ ἀπ᾽ αὐτῶν ποιεῖσθαι they asked whether they should deliver their city to the Corinthians, and should try.., [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.25:]] —in both constructions the _indicative_ or subjunctive may be retained, ψῆφον ἐβούλοντο ἐπαγαγεῖν εἰ χρὴ πολεμεῖν[Refs [[prev. work] 119]]; ἐβουλεύοντο εἴτε κατακαύσωσιν.. εἴτε τι ἄλλο χρήσωνται whether they should burn them or should dispose of them in some other way, [Refs [[prev. author] 2.4]]; ἀνακοινοῦσθαι αὐτὸν αὑτῷ εἰ δῷ ἐπιψηφίσαι τοῖς προέδροις [he said that] he consulted him whether he should give.., [Refs 4th c.BC+ [4th c.BC: Aeschines Orator 2.68.]]

__C.4
with OPT. and ἄν when this was the form of the direct question, ἠρώτων εἰ δοῖεν ἂν τούτων τὰ πιστά they asked whether they would give (direct δοιήτε ἄ;), [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 4.8.7.]]

__C.5
the NEG. used with εἰ in indirect questions is οὐ, when οὐ would be used in the direct question, ἐνετέλλετο.. εἰρωτᾶν εἰ οὔ τι ἐπαισχύνεται whether he is not ashamed, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.90, etc.]]; but if μή would be required in the direct form, it is retained in the indirect, οὐ τοῦτο ἐρωτῶ, ἀλλ᾽ εἰ τοῦ μὲν δικαίου μὴ ἀξιοῖ πλέον ἔχειν μηδὲ βούλεται ὁ δίκαιος, τοῦ δὲ ἀδίκου (the direct question would be μὴ ἀξιοῖ μηδὲ βούλετα; he does not see fit nor wish, does he?) short_definition: hero — 1. a hero, in (Homer) used of the Greeks before Troy, then of warriors generally; and then of all free men of the heroic age, as the minstrel Demodocus, the herald Mulius, even the
deep_entry:
Abbott-Smith / STEPBible (TBESG)
1. a hero, in (Homer) used of the Greeks before Troy, then of warriors  generally; and then of all free men of the heroic age, as the minstrel Demodocus, the herald Mulius, even the unwarlike Phaeacians.
2. in (Hesiod) the blessed heroes  are the fourth age of men, who fell before Thebes and Troy, and then passed to the Islands of the Blest.
3. heroes, as objects of worship, demigods  or men born from a god and a mortal, as Hercules, Aeneas, Memnon, (Herdotus Historicus); then of such as had done great services to mankind, as Daedalus, Triptolemus, Theseus, [variant datesAnthology Palantina
4. later, the heroes are inferior local deities , patrons of tribes, cities, guilds, founders of cities, etc.; as at Athens, the ἥρωες ἐπώνυμοι were the heroes after whom the  φυλαί were named , (Herdotus Historicus) (ML)

ἐπεμβῆναι ποδί 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Electra” 456]]; πόδα βαίνειν, see at {βαίνω} [Refs 4th c.BC+ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus 11.4]]; πόδα τιθέναι to journey, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Thesmophoriazusae” 1100: _metaphorically_, νόστιμον ναῦς ἐκίνησεν πόδα]] started on its homeward way, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Hecuba” 940 (Lyric poetry); νεῶν λῦσαι ποθοῦσιν οἴκαδ᾽.. πόδα [prev. work] 1020]]; χειρῶν ἔκβαλλον ὀρείους πόδας ναός, i. e. oars, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Timotheus Lyricus “Persae” 102]]; φωνὴ τῶν π. τοῦ ὑετοῦ sound of the pattering of rain, [LXX.3Ki.18.41.]

__3
as a point of measurement, ἐς πόδας ἐκ κεφαλῆς from head to foot, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 18.353; ἐκ κεφαλῆς ἐς πόδας ἄκρους 16.640; and reversely, ἐκ ποδῶν δ᾽ ἄνω.. εἰς ἄκρον κάρα 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Fragmenta - American Journal of Philology” 169; ἐκ τῶν ποδῶν ἐς τὴν κεφαλήν σοι 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Plutus” 650; also ἐκ τριχὸς ἄχρι ποδῶν “Anthologia Graeca” 5.193 (3rd c.BC: Posidippus Comicus or 3rd c.BC: Asclepiades Epigrammaticus); ἐς κορυφὰν ἐκ ποδός [prev. work] 7.388 (from Bianor).]]

__4
πρόσθε ποδός or ποδῶν, προπάροιθε ποδῶν, just before one, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 23.877, 21.601, 13.205; τὸ πρὸ ποδὸς.. χρῆμα 5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “I.” 8(7).13; αὐτὰ τὰ πρὸ τῶν ποδῶν ὁρᾶν 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Respublica Lacedaemoniorum” 3.4, compare “An.” 4.6.12, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 432d.]]

__4.b
παρά or πὰρ ποδός off-hand, at once, ἀνελέσθαι πὰρ ποδός [Refs 6th c.BC+ [6th c.BC: Theognis Elegiacus 282; γνόντα τὸ πὰρ ποδός 5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “P.” 3.60, compare 10.62; πὰρ ποδί]]close at hand, [Refs [[prev. author] “O.” 1.74]]; but παραὶ ποσὶ κάππεσε θυμός sank to their feet, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 15.280; παρὰ πόδα]]in a moment, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 838 (Lyric poetry), 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Sophista” 242a]]; close behind, Νέμεσις δέ γε πὰρ πόδας (to be read πόδα) βαίνει Prov. cited in [Refs [10th c.AD: Suidas Legal icographus]]; also παρὰ πόδας immediately afterwards [Refs 2nd c.BC+ [2nd c.BC: Polybius Historicus 1.35.3, 5.26.13, 2nd c.AD: Galenus Medicus 5.272; παρὰ π. οἱ ἔλεγχοι 2nd c.AD: Lucianus Sophista “Hist. Conscr.” 13, compare 2nd c.AD: Aristides Rhetor 2.115 1st c.AD: Josephus Historicus]]; τὰ ἔμπροσθεν αὐτοῦ καὶ παρὰ πόδας at his very feet, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Theaetetus” 174a; περὶ τῶν παρὰ πόδας καὶ τῶν ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς [prev. work]c; τὸ πλησίον καὶ παρὰ π. 2nd c.AD: Lucianus Sophista “Cal.” 1.]]

__4.c
ἐν ποσί in one's way, close at hand, τὸν ἐν π. γινόμενον [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 3.79, compare 5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “P.” 8.32; τἀν ποσὶν κακά 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Antigone” 1327, compare 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Andromache” 397; τοὐν ποσὶν κακόν [prev. author] Alcaeus739; τὴν ἐν ποσὶ [κώμην] αἱρεῖν 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 3.97; τὰ ἐν ποσὶν ἀγνοεῖν]]everyday matters, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Theaetetus” 175b, compare 4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “Politica” 1263a18, etc.]]

__4.d
τὸ πρὸς ποσί, ={τὸ ἐν ποσί}, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Tyrannus” 130.]]

__4.e
all these phrases are opposed to ἐκ ποδῶν out of the way, far off, written ἐκποδών [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 6.35, etc.; also, βίαια πάντ᾽ ἐκ ποδὸς ἐρύσαις 5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “N.” 7.67.]]

__5
to denote close pursuit, ἐκ ποδὸς ἕπεσθαι follow in the track, i.e. close behind, [Refs 2nd c.BC+ [2nd c.BC: Polybius Historicus 3.68.1, compare 1st c.BC: Diodorus Siculus Historicus 20.57, 1st c.BC: Dionysius Halicarnassensis 2.33, etc.; ἐκ ποδῶν διώξαντες 1st-2nd c.AD: Plutarchus Biographus et Philosophus “Pelopidas” 11.]]

__5.b
in earlier writers κατὰ πόδας on the heels of a person, [LXX+5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 5.98, 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 3.98, 8.17, 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Historia Graeca (Hellenica)” 2.1.20, LXX.Gen.49.19 (also κατὰ πόδα ὑπολαβεῖν]]on the moment, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Sophista” 243d)]]; ἡ κατὰ πόδας ἡμέρα the very next day, [Refs 2nd c.BC+ [2nd c.BC: Polybius Historicus 1.12.1 (but κατὰ πόδας αἱρεῖν]] catch it running, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 1.6.40, compare “Mem.” 2.6.9): with _genitive_ _person_, κατὰ πόδας τινὸς ἐλαύνειν, ἰέναι,]] march, come close at his heels, on his track, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 9.89, 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 5.64]]; τῇ κατὰ π. ἡμέρᾳ τῆς ἐκκλησίας on the day immediately after it, [Refs 2nd c.BC+ [2nd c.BC: Polybius Historicus 3.45.5; κατὰ π. τῆς μάχης 2nd c.AD: Aristides Rhetor 1.157J., etc.]]

__6
various phrases:

__6.a
ἀνὰ πόδα backwards, [Refs 5th c.AD+ [5th c.AD(?): Hesychius Legal icographus]]

__6.b
ἐπὶ πόδα backwards facing the enemy, ἐπὶ π. ἀναχωρεῖν, ἀνάγειν, ἀναχάζεσθαι, to retire without turning to fly, leisurely, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 5.2.32, “Cyr.” 3.3.69, 7.1.34, etc.; also ἐπὶ πόδας 2nd c.AD: Lucianus Sophista “Pisc.” 12]]; but γίνεται ἡ ἔξοδος οἷον ἐπὶ πόδας the offspring is as it were born feetforemost, [Refs 4th c.BC+ [4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “de Generatione Animalium” 752b14.]]

__6.c
περὶ πόδα, properly of a shoe, round the foot, i.e. fitting exactly, ὡς ἔστι μοι τὸ χρῆμα τοῦτο περὶ πόδα [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Comicus 197, compare 129: with _dative_, ὁρᾷς ὡς ἐμμελὴς ἡ ἀρχὴ καὶ περὶ πόδα τῇ ἱστορίᾳ 2nd c.AD: Lucianus Sophista “Hist.Conscr.” 14, compare “Ind.” 10, “Pseudol.” 23.]]

__6.d
ὡς ποδῶνἔχει as he is off for feet, i. e. as quick as he can, ὡς ποδῶν εἶχον [τάχιστα] ἐβοήθεον [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 6.116; ἐδίωκον ὡς ποδῶν ἕκαστος εἶχον [prev. author] 9.59; φευκτέον ὡς ἔχει ποδῶν ἕκαστος 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Gorgias” 507d; so, σοῦσθε.. ὅπως ποδῶν [ἔχετε] 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Supplices” 837 (Lyric poetry).]]

__6.e
ἔξω τινὸς πόδα ἔχειν keep one's foot out of a thing, i. e. be clear of it, ἔξω κομίζων πηλοῦ πόδα [Refs 5th c.BC+ [[prev. author] “Ch.” 697; πημάτων ἔξω πόδα ἔχει [prev. author] “Pr.” 265; ἐκτὸς κλαυμάτων 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 1260; ἔξω πραγμάτων 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Heraclidae” 109: without a _genitive_, ἐκτὸς ἔχειν πόδα 5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “P.” 4.289: opposed to εἰς ἄντλον ἐμβήσῃ πόδα 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Heraclidae” 168; ἐν τούτῳ πεδίλῳ.. πόδ᾽ ἔχων 5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “O.” 6.8.]]

__6.f
ἀμφοῖν ποδοῖν, etc., to denote energetic action, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Aves” 35, compare 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 13.78; συνέχευε ποσὶν καὶ χερσὶν 15.364; χερσίν τε ποσίν τε καὶ σθένει 20.360; τιμωρήσειν χειρὶ καὶ ποδὶ καὶ πάσῃ δυνάμει 4th c.BC: Aeschines Orator 2.115, compare 3.109]]; τερπωλῆς ἐπέβημεν ὅλῳ ποδί with all the foot, i.e. entirely, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [3rd c.BC: Apollonius Rhodius Epicus 4.1166, compare 1st-2nd c.AD: Dio Chrysostomus Sophista 13.19 (probably); καταφεύγειν ἐπὶ τὴν πόλιν ὥσπερ ἐκ δυοῖν ποδοῖν 2nd c.AD: Aristides Rhetor 1.117J.; opposed to οὐκ ἂν προβαίην τὸν πόδα τὸν ἕτερον 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Ecclesiazusae” 161; οὐκ ἂν ἔφασκεν ἐξελθεῖν οὐδὲ τὸν ἕτερον πόδα 4th-3rd c.BC: Dinarchus Orator 1.82.]]

__6.g
τὴν ὑπὸ πόδα [κατάστασιν] just below them, [Refs 2nd c.BC+ [2nd c.BC: Polybius Historicus 2.68.9]]; ὑπὸ πόδας τίθεσθαι trample under foot, scorn, [Refs 1st c.AD+ [1st-2nd c.AD: Plutarchus Biographus et Philosophus 2.1097c]]; οἱ ὑπὸ πόδα those next below them (in rank), [Refs 1st c.AD+ [1st c.AD: Onosander (Onasander) Tacticus 25.2]]; ὑπὸ πόδα χωρεῖν recede, decline, of strength, [Refs 2nd c.AD+ [2nd c.AD: Athenaeus Epigrammaticus]] middle cited in [Refs 4th c.AD+ [4th c.AD: Oribasius Medicus (?) 21.16.]]

__6.h
for ὀρθῷ ποδί, see at {ὀρθός} [Refs [II.1.]]

__6.k
ἁλιεῖς ἀπὸ ποδός probably fishermen who fish from the land, not from boats, [Refs 2nd c.AD+ [“BGU” 221.5 (2nd-3rd c.AD)]]; ποτίσαι ἀπὸ ποδός perhaps irrigate by the feet (of oxen turning the irrigation-wheel), [Refs 2nd c.AD+ [“PRyl.” 157.21 (2nd c.AD)]]; τόπον.. ἀπὸ ποδὸς ἐξηρτισμένον uncertain meaning in [Refs 2nd c.AD+ [“POsl.” 55.11 (2nd-3rd c.AD).]]

__1
ἀγγεῖον.. τρήματα ἐκ τῶν ὑπὸ ποδὸς ἔχον round the bottom, [Refs 1st c.AD+ [1st c.AD: Dioscorides (Dioscurides) Medicus 2.72.]]

__7
πούς τινος, as periphrastic for a person as coming, etc., σὺν πατρὸς μολὼν ποδί, i.e. σὺν πατρί, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Hippolytus” 661; παρθένου δέχου πόδα [prev. author] “Or.” 1217, compare “Hec.” 977, “HF” 336; χρόνου πόδα [prev. author] “Ba.” 889 (Lyric poetry), 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Ranae” 100]]; also ἐξ ἑνὸς ποδός, i.e. μόνος ὤν, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 91]]; οἱ δ᾽ ἀφ᾽ ἡσύχου π., i.e. οἱ ἡσύχως ζῶντες, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Medea” 217.]]

__II
metaphorically, of things, foot, lowest part, especially foot of a hill, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 2.824, 20.59 (_plural_), 5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “P.” 11.36, etc.]]; of a table, couch, etc., [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Fragmenta” 530, 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 8.8.16, etc.]]; compare πέζ; of the side strokes at the foot of the letter Ω, Callias cited in [Refs 2nd c.AD+ [2nd c.AD: Athenaeus Epigrammaticus 10.454a]]; ={ποδεών}[Refs 5th c.BC+ [11.1, ἀσκοῦ.. λῦσαι π. 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Medea” 679.]]

__II.2
in a ship, πόδες are the two lower corners of the sail, or the ropes fastened therelo, by which the sails are tightened or slackened, sheets [Refs 8th c.BC+ [compare (ποδεών 11.4), 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 5.260]]; χαλᾶν πόδα ease off the sheet, as is done when a squall is coming, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Orestes” 707]]; τοῦ ποδὸς παρίει let go hold of it, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Equites” 436; ἐκδοῦναι ὀλίγον τοῦ ποδός 2nd c.AD: Lucianus Sophista “Cont.” 3]]; ἐκπετάσουσι πόδα ναός (with reference to the sail), [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Iphigenia Taurica” 1135 (Lyric poetry): opposed to τεῖναι πόδα]] haul it tight, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Antigone” 715]]; ναῦς ἐνταθεῖσα ποδί a ship with her sheet close hauled, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Orestes” 706; κὰδ᾽ δ᾽.. λαῖφος ἐρυσσάμενοι τανύοντο ἐς πόδας ἀμφοτέρους 3rd c.BC: Apollonius Rhodius Epicus 2.932; ἱστία.. ἐτάνυσσαν ὑπ᾽ ἀμφοτέροισι πόδεσσι 4th c.AD(?): Quintus Smyrnaeus Epicus 9.438.]]

__II.2.b
perhaps of the rudder or steering-paddle, αἰεὶ γὰρ πόδα νηὸς ἐνώμων [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 10.32 (cf. Scholia (at [prev. work])); πὰρ ποδὶ ναός 5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “N.” 6.55.]]

__III
a foot, as a measure of length, = [Refs 5th c.BC+ [4 palms (παλασταί) or 6 fingers, 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 2.149, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Meno” 82c, etc.]]

__IV
foot in Prosody, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Ranae” 1323 (Lyric poetry), 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 400a, 4th c.BC: Aristoxenus Musicus “Harmonica” p.34 M., 7th c.AD: Hephaestio Grammaticus 3.1, etc.]]; so of a metrical phrase or passage, ἔκμετρα καὶ ὑπὲρ τὸν π. [Refs 2nd c.AD+ [2nd c.AD: Lucianus Sophista “Pr.Im.” 18]]; of a long passage declaimed in one breath, κήρυκες ὅταν τὸν καλούμενον πόδα μέλλωσιν ἐρεῖν [Refs 2nd c.AD+ [2nd c.AD: Galenus Medicus 4.459, compare 2nd c.AD: Lucianus Sophista “Demon.” 65, 2nd c.AD(?): Pollianus Epigrammaticus 4.91.]]

__V
boundary stone, [Refs 4th c.BC+ [4th c.BC: Isaeus Orator “fragment” 27]]. (Cf. Latin pes, Gothic fotus, etc. 'foot'; related to πέδον as noted by [Refs 4th c.BC+ [4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “de Incessu Animalium” 706a33.)]]

καταβο-άω,
future -βοήσομαι[Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Equites” 286]]; Ionic dialect -βώσομαι[Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 6.85: strengthened for βοάω]]:—bawl, οὐ μόνον βοᾶν, ἀλλ᾽ ἤδη καὶ καταβοᾶν [Refs 1st c.AD+ [1st c.AD: Philo Judaeus 1.475: but usually]]

__2
with genitive, cry out, inveigh against, τινὸς περί τινος [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus [same place]; κ. τινῶν ὅτι σπονδὰς λελυκότες εἶεν 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.67, compare 115, 5.45]]:—passive, have clamour raised against one, ὑπό τινων [Refs 2nd c.AD+ [2nd c.AD: Appianus Historicus “Bella Civilia” 5.13.]]

__II

II), (Herdotus Historicus):—;of persons, καταδεδυκώς having popped down , (Aristophanes Comicus)
2. to go down into, plunge into , with accusative, καταδῦναι ὅμιλον, μάχην, δόμον, πόλιν (Homer); followed by a preposition, καταδυσόμεθ᾽ εἰς Ἀί̈δαο δόμους we will go down  into . ., (Odyssey by Homer), etc.:—;with a notion of secresy, to insinuate oneself, steal into , (Plato Philosophus)
3. to slink away and lie hid , καταδύομαι ὑπὸ τῆς αἰσχύνης (Xenophon Historicus)
4. to get into, put on , τεύχεα (Homer)
5. Causal, to make to sink , Lat. submergere, ἐμὲ καταδύουσι τῷ ἄχει (Xenophon Historicus); mostly in aor1, τοὺς γαυλοὺς καταδύσας (Herdotus Historicus); καταδῦσαι ναῦν to cut  it down to the water's edge, disable  it, (Herdotus Historicus) (ML)

__I.2
go down, plunge into, with accusative, καταδῦναι ὅμιλον [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 10.231, etc.]]; κατεδύσετο πουλὺν ὅμιλον[Refs 8th c.BC+ [[prev. work] 517; καταδύσεο μῶλον Ἄρηος 18.134; so μάχην, δόμον, πόλιν καταδύμεναι, 3.241, 8.375, 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 4.246: followed by _preposition_, μυῖαι καδδῦσαι (_Epic dialect_ for καταδ-) κατὰ.. ὠτειλάς 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 19.25; σπάργαν᾽ ἔσω κατέδυνε “hymnus ad Mercurium” 237]]; καταδυσόμεθ᾽.. εἰς Ἀΐδαο δόμους we shall go down into.., [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 10.174; so καταδύνειν ἐς ὕλην 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 9.37, compare 4.76]]; εἰς φάραγγας, of hares, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Cynegeticus” 5.16]]; εἰς ἅπασαν [τὴν πόλιν] [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 576e; κατὰ τῆς γῆς 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 4.132; κατὰ τέφρας πολλῆς 1st-2nd c.AD: Plutarchus Biographus et Philosophus “Camillus” 32]]; of souls, εἰς βυθὸν κ. __I.3

short_definition: hollow — 1. hollow, hollowed , epithet of ships, which in early times were hollowed out of trees, (Homer); later, κοίλη ναῦς was the hold of the ship, (Herdotus Historicus); so, ἡ κοίλη alo
deep_entry:
Abbott-Smith / STEPBible (TBESG)
1. hollow, hollowed , epithet of ships, which in early times were hollowed out of trees, (Homer); later, κοίλη ναῦς was the hold  of the ship, (Herdotus Historicus); so, ἡ κοίλη alone, (Theocritus Poeta Bucolicus):—;of the Trojan horse, κ. λόχος, κ. δόρυ (Odyssey by Homer); κ. κάπετος, of a grave, (Iliad by Homer); κ. δέμνια, of the bed when no one is in it , (Sophocles Tragicus)
2. of Places, lying in a hollow  or forming a hollow , κοίλη Λακεδαίμων the vale  of L., (Odyssey by Homer); κ. Θεσσαλία (Herdotus Historicus); κ. Ἄργος (Sophocles Tragicus); τὰ Κοῖλα τῆς Εὐβοίας (Herdotus Historicus); ἡ Κοιλή the valley  of the Ilissus, (Herdotus Historicus):—; κ. λιμήν of a harbour lying between high cliffs , (Odyssey by Homer); κ. αἰγιαλός an embayed  beach, (Odyssey by Homer):—; κ. ὁδός a hollow  way, (Iliad by Homer):—; κ. ποταμός a river nearly empty  of water, (Thucydides) (so Virgil, cava flumina) : metaphorically of the voice, hollow , μυκάσατο κοῖλον (Theocritus Poeta Bucolicus); φθέγγεσθαι κοῖλον (Lucian)
3. as Substantive κοῖλον, ου, τό, a hollow, cavity, ravine , (Plato Philosophus); like κοιλία, of the cavities  in the body, τὰ κ. γαστρός (Euripides); also, ἐν τῷ κοίλῳ καὶ μυχῷ τοῦ λιμένος (Thucydides) (ML)

μέν used absolutely to express certainty, not followed by correlative δέ, indeed, of a truth, synonymous with μήν, as appears from the Epic dialect and Ionic dialect form ἦ μέν in protestations and oaths (where Attic dialect used ἦ μήν), καί μοι ὄμοσσον, ἦ μ. μοι πρόφρων ἔπεσιν καὶ χερσὶν ἀρήξειν [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.77, compare 14.275; ἦ μέν τοι τάδε πάντα τελείεται 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 14.160, compare 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 24.416; τοῦτον ἐξορκοῖ, ἦ μέν οἱ διηκονήσειν 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 4.154, compare 5.93, etc.: with _negative_, οὐ μὲν γάρ τι κακὸν βασιλευέμεν 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 1.392, etc.; ὤμοσα, μὴ μὲν.. ἀναφῆναι 4.254, compare 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 2.118, 179; ἔξαρνος ἦν, μὴ μὲν ἀποκτεῖναι [prev. author] 3.67, compare 99: without _negative_, ἀνδρὸς μὲν τόδε σῆμα πάλαι κατατεθνηῶτος 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 7.89]]: also in Trag., ἀκτὴ μὲν ἥδε τῆς περιρρύτου χθονός [Refs 8th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 1, compare 159 (_anapaest meter_), “OC” 44, 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Medea” 676, 1129, etc.; καὶ μέν 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.269, 9.632, etc.; οὐδὲ μὲν οὐδὲ.. 2.703, 12.212]]; γε μέν, compare γε [Refs [1.5.]]

__A.I.2
an answering clause with δέ is sometimes implied, τὴν μὲν ἐγὼ σπουδῇ δάμνημ᾽ ἐπέεσσι her can I hardly subdue, [but all others easily], [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 5.893]]; ὡς μὲν λέγουσι as indeed they say, [but as I believe not], [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Orestes” 8]]; καὶ πρῶτον μὲν ἦν αὐτῷ πόλεμος (with no ἔπειτα δέ to follow), [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 1.9.14]]; so νῦν μέν σ᾽ ἀφήσω I will let you go this time, [Refs 3rd c.BC+ [3rd c.BC: Herodas Mimographus 5.81]]: to give force to assertions made by a person respecting himself, wherein opposition to other persons is implied, ὡς μὲν ἐμῷ θυμῷ δοκεῖ [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 13.154]]; δοκεῖν μέν μοι ἥξει τήμερον [τὸ πλοῖον] [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Crito” 43d]]: hence with the person pronoun, ἐγὼ μέν νυν θεοῖσι ἔχω χάριν [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.71]]; ἐγὼ μὲν οὐδέν (i.e. θέλω) [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Antigone” 498; ἐμοῦ μὲν οὐχ ἑκόντος [prev. author] “Aj.” 455; ἐγὼ μὲν οὐκ οἶδα 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 1.4.12, compare 4.2.45, etc.]]: with the demonstrative pronoun, τούτου μὲν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐγὼ σοφώτερός εἰμι [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Apologia” 21d: generally, to emphasize the preceding word, πολλὴ μὲν ἡ μεταβολή μοι γέγονεν]] great indeed has been the change, [Refs 4th c.BC+ [4th c.BC: Isaeus Orator 1.1, compare 4th-5th c.BC: Simonides Lyricus 5.1, etc.]]

__A.I.3
μέν is used alone in questions, when the answer is assumed, I take it, θέμις μὲν ἡμᾶς χρησμὸν εἰδέναι θεο; [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Medea” 676, compare “Ion” 520 (troch.), “Hipp.” 316, 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Antigone” 634, 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Aves” 1214]]; Ἕλλην μέν ἐστι καὶ Ἑλληνίζε; [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Meno” 82b.]]

__A.II
μέν followed by δέ in the correlative clause or clauses, on the one hand, on the other hand; commonly in Classical Gr., less frequently in later Gr. (rare in NT

__A.II.1
μέν.., δέ.. (or when the correlative clause is negative, μέν.., οὐδέ.., [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.318, 536)]], to mark opposition, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus, etc.]]—The opposed clauses commonly stand together, but are frequently separated by clauses, parenthetic or explanatory; e.g. μέν in [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 2.494 is answered by δέ in 511, 527f]]; in [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 1.9.2, πρῶτον μέν is answered by ἐπεὶ δέ]] in  6; in [prev. author] “Mem.” 1.1.2, πρῶτον μέν is answered by θαυμαστὸν δέ in 1.2.1.]]

__A.II.2
to connect a series of clauses containing different matter, though with no opposition, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.18s q., 306f (five δέ-clauses), 433f (eight δέ-clauses),compare 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 1.3.14, 7.10s q.: frequently when the members of a group or class are distinctly specified, παῖδες δύο, πρεσβύτερος μὲν Ἀρταξέρξης, νεώτερος δὲ Κῦρος [prev. work] 1.1.1; τάφρος.., τὸ μὲν εὖρος ὀργυιαὶ πέντε, τὸ δὲ βάθος ὀργυιαὶ τρεῖς [prev. work] 1.7.14; πρῶτος μέν.., δεύτερος δέ.., τρίτος δέ.. [prev. work] 5.6.9]]; τότε μέν.., τότε δέ.., at one time.., at another.., [Refs [[prev. work] 6.1.9, etc.: especially with the _Article_ used as a _pronoun_,]] ὁ μέν.., ὁ δέ..; τὸ μέν.., τὸ δέ.., etc.

__A.II.3
the principal word is frequently repeated, οἳ περὶ μὲν βουλὴν Δαναῶν, περὶ δ᾽ ἐστὲ μάχεσθαι [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.258, compare 288, 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 15.70; ἔνι μὲν φιλότης, ἐν δ᾽ ἵμερος, ἐν δ᾽ ὀαριστύς 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 14.216; Ξέρξης μὲν ἄγαγεν.., Ξέρξης δ᾽ ἀπώλεσεν 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Persae” 550, compare 560, 694, 700 (all Lyric poetry)]]; χαλεπαίνει μὲν πρῳρεύς, χαλεπαίνει δὲ κυβερνήτης [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 5.8.20.]]

__A.II.4
one of the correlative clauses is sometimes independent, while the other takes the participle or some other dependent form, ἐβλασφήμει κατ᾽ ἐμοῦ.., μάρτυρα μὲν.. οὐδένα παρασχόμενος.., παρεκελεύετο δέ.. [Refs 5th c.BC+ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 57.11; οἱ ἀμφὶ βασιλέα, πεζοὶ μὲν οὐκέτι, τῶν δὲ ἱππέων ὁ λόφος ἐνεπλήσθη 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 1.10.12, compare 2.1.7, 5.6.29; ὧν ἐπιμεμφομένα σ᾽ ἁδεῖα μὲν ἀντία δ᾽ οἴσω 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Trachiniae” 123, compare “OC” 522 (bothlyr.); χωρὶς μὲν τοῦ ἐστερῆσθαι.., ἔτι δὲ καὶ.. δόξω ἀμελῆσαι 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Crito” 44]] b.

__A.II.5
μέν and δέ frequently oppose two clauses, whereof one is subordinate to the other in meaning or emphasis, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [ἀλλ᾽ ἐκεῖνο θαυμάζω, εἰ Λακεδαιμονίοις μέν ποτε.. ἀντήρατε,.. νυνὶ δὲ ὀκνεῖτ᾽ ἐξιέναι (for εἰ.. ἀντάραντες νυνὶ ὀκνεῖτε) 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 2.24, compare 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Iphigenia Taurica” 116, 5th c.BC: Lysias Orator 34.11, 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Memorabilia” 2.7.11, etc.]]: so in an anacoluthon, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [τρία μὲν ὄντα.. ναυτικά.., τούτων δ᾽ εἰ περιόψεσθε τὰ δύο, κτλ., 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.36.]]

__A.II.6
μέν is not always answered by δέ, but frequently by other equivalent Particles, as ἀλλά, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.22f, 2.703f, 5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “O.” 9.1, 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Persae” 176, 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 1.7.17:—by μέντοι, 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.36, 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 350, 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 21.189, etc.:—by ἀτάρ, 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 6.84, 124, 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Prometheus Vinctus” 342, 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Tyrannus” 1051s q., 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Theaetetus” 172c, etc. (so μέν.., αὐτάρ]] in Epic dialect, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.50, 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 19.513, etc.):— by αὖ, 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 11.108, 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 4.210:—by αὖθις, 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Antigone” 165:—by αὖτε, 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.234, 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 22.5:—by temporal Particles, πρῶτα μέν.., εἶτα.. 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Electra” 261]]; πρῶτον μέν.., μετὰ τοῦτο.. [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 6.1.5 - 7]]; μάλιστα μὲν δὴ.., ἔπειτα μέντοι.. [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 350, compare “OT” 647:]] —rarely by μήν with negative, οὐδὲν μὴν κωλύει [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedrus” 268e; οὐ μὴν αὐταί γε [prev. author] “Phlb.” 12d.]]

__A.II.6.b
when the opposition is emphatic, δέ is sometimes strengthened, as ὅμως δέ.. [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Tyrannus” 785, “Ph.” 473, 1074, etc. (so ἀλλ᾽ ὅμως “El.” 450)]]; δ᾽ αὖ.. [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 4.415, 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 1.10.5]]; δ᾽ ἔμπης.. [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.561 - 2.]]

__A.II.6.c
μέν is sometimes answered by a copulative Particle, κάρτιστοι μὲν ἔσαν καὶ καρτίστοις ἐμάχοντο[Refs 8th c.BC+ [[prev. work] 267, compare 459, 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 22.475, 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Ajax” 1, “Tr.” 689, 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Medea” 125 (_anapaest meter_)]], etc.: rarely in Prose, τρία μὲν ἔτη ἀντεῖχον.., καὶ οὐ πρότερον ἐνέδοσαν [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 2.65 (uncertain).]]

where each Particle retains its force,

μὲν ἄρα, in [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus μέν ῥα, 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 2.1, 6.312, 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 1.127, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedrus” 258d, “R.” 467d, etc.]]

μὲν δή [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.514, 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.32, etc.]]: frequently used to express positive certainty, ἀλλ᾽ οἶσθα μὲν δή [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Trachiniae” 627, compare “OT” 294; τὰ μὲν δὴ τόξ᾽ ἔχεις [prev. author] “Ph.” 1308]]; especially as a conclusion, τοῦτο μὲν δὴ.. ὁμολογεῖται [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Gorgias” 470b, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 1.1.6, etc.]]: in closing a statement, τοιαῦτα μὲν δὴ ταῦτα [Refs 8th c.BC+ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Prometheus Vinctus” 500, etc.: used in answers to convey full assent, ἦ μὲν δή (compare supr. A) 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 9.348, 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 4.33; καὶ μὲν δή.. γε 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 409b]]; οὐ μὲν δή, to deny positively, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 8.238, 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 1.6.9, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Theaetetus” 148e, etc.; οὐ μὲν δή.. γε 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 2.2.3, 3.2.14]]; ἀλλ᾽ οὔ τι μὲν δή.. __B.II
where the Particles combine so as to form a new sense,

__B.II.1

μὲν οὖν is frequently used with a corresponding δέ, so that each Particle retains its force, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 4.780, 5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “O.” 1.111, 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Tyrannus” 244, 843; “Ph.” 359, 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 2.5, etc.]]: but frequently also absolutely, so then, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Antigone” 65; ταῦτα μὲν οὖν παραλείψω 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 2.3]]; especially in replies, sometimes in strong affirmation, παντάπασι μὲν οὖν [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Theaetetus” 158d; κομιδῇ μὲν οὖν [prev. work] 159e; πάνυ μὲν οὖν [prev. work] 159b; ἀνάγκη μὲν οὖν [prev. work] 189e]]; also to substitute a new statement so as to correct a preceding statement, nay rather, κακοδαίμω; Answ. βαρυδαίμων μὲν οὖν! by μέν τε, if δέ τε follows, the two clauses are more closely combined than by τε.., τε.., [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 5.139, +others; μέν τε is frequently answered by δέ alone, 16.28, +others]]; by ἀλλά, αὐτάρ,[Refs 8th c.BC+ [17.727, 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 1.215, +others]]; perhaps by ἠδέ, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 4.341:— 8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus also uses μέν τε]] absolutely, when τε loses its force, as after ἦ, τίς, etc., [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 2.145, +others]]

μέν τοι in [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus]] always occurs in speeches, where τοι can be regarded as the dative of the pronoun: later, μέντοι is written as a single word, and is used:

μέντοι γε [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 5.5.24, etc.; οὐ μ. γε 5th c.BC: Diogenes Apolloniates Philosophus 5: in later Gr. μέντοιγε]] stands first in the sentence, μ. οὐ θέλω [Refs 1st c.AD+ [“PLond.” 3.897.13 (1st c.AD)]]; also γε μέντοι [Refs 5th c.BC+ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Agamemnon” 938, 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Tyrannus” 778, 1292, 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Hecuba” 600; ὅμως γε μ. 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Ranae” 61.]]

__D
Position of μέν. Like δέ, it usually stands as the second word in a sentence. But when a sentence begins with words common to its subordinate clauses, μέν stands second in the first of these clauses, as ἥδε γὰρ γυνὴ δούλη μέν, εἴρηκεν δ᾽ ἐλεύθερον λόγον [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Trachiniae” 63]]; οἱ Ἀθηναῖοι ἐτάξαντο μέν.., ἡσύχαζον δέ.. [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 4.73, compare 113, etc. It also attaches itself to words which mark opposition, as πρῶτον μέν, τότε μέν, ἐγὼ μέν]], even when these do not stand first: sometimes however it precedes them, ὡς μὲν ἐγὼ οἶμαι [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedrus” 228b; ὡς μέν τινες ἔφασαν 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 5.2.28]]. It generally stands between the Article and Noun, or the preposition and its Case: but if special stress is laid on the Noun, this is sometimes neglected, as οἱ Τεγεᾶται μὲν ἐπηυλίσαντο, Μαντινῆς δὲ ἀπεχώρησαν [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 4.134]]; ἀνὰ τὸ σκοτεινὸν μέν.. [Refs 5th c.BC+ [[prev. author] 3.22; also τῇ σῇ μὲν εὐδαιμονίῃ, τῇ ἐμεωυτοῦ δὲ κακοδαιμονίῃ 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.87]].

__D.II
μέν is frequently repeated:

__D.II.1
when, besides the opposition of two main clauses, a subordinate opposition is introduced into the first, ὁ μὲν ἀνὴρ τοιαῦτα μὲν πεποίηκε τοιαῦτα δὲ λέγει, ὑμῶν δέ.. [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 1.6.9, compare 5.8.24, 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 8.104, 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 18.214, 23.208.]]

__D.II.2
in apodosi with the demonstrative pronoun or adverb, τὸν μὲν καλέουσι θέρος, τοῦτον μὲν προσκυνέουσι, τὸν δὲ χειμῶνα[Refs 5th c.BC+ [.. 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 2.121; ὅσοι μὲν δὴ νομοῦ τοῦ Θηβαίου εἰσί, οὗτοι μέν [νυν].. αἶγας θύουσι· ὅσοι δὲ.. νομοῦ τοῦ Μενδησίου εἰσί, οὗτοι δὲ.. ὄϊς θύουσι [prev. work] 42, compare 3.108, +others]]; ὅτε μέν με οἱ ἄρχοντες ἔταττον.., τότε μὲν ἔμενον.., τοῦ δὲ θεοῦ τάττοντος,.. ἐνταῦθα δέ.. [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Apologia” 28e, compare “Grg.” 512a.]]

__D.II.3
μέν used absolutely is frequently followed by a correlative μέν, εἰ μὲν οὖν ἡμεῖς μὲν.. ποιοῦμεν [Refs [[prev. author] “R.” 421a.]]

__D.III
μέν is sometimes omitted (especially in Poetry) where it is implied in the following δέ, φεύγων, ὁ δ᾽ ὄπισθε διώκων [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 22.157; ἐλευθεροῦτε πατρίδ᾽, ἐλευθεροῦτε δὲ παῖδας 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Persae” 403; σφραγῖδε.. χρυσοῦν ἔχουσα τὸν δακτύλιον, ἡ δ᾽ ἑτέρα ἀργυροῦν “IG” 22.1388.45, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Nubes” 396, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Sophista” 221e, 4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “Poetica” 1447b14, etc.]]

poet. Verb, active (intransitive) only in present and imperfect (Epic dialect ναίεσκον [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 5.708),]]future and aorist in causal and middle and passive forms, see below [Refs [11, 111:]]

__1
of persons, dwell, abide, mostly followed by a preposition of Place, ἐν Λῃ, etc., Il.[same place], etc.; ῥοῇς ἔπι Σαγγαρίοιο [Refs 8th c.BC+ [16.719; ἐπ᾽ ἄκρων ὀρέων 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Tyrannus” 1105 (Lyric poetry); κατὰ πτόλιν 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 2.130; ἀν᾽ οὔρεα 8th-7th c.BC: Hesiodus Epicus “Theogonia” 130; πὰρ ποταμόν 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 2.522; ὑπὸ Πλάκῳ 6.396: with _dative_ loci, αἰθέρι ναίων 2.412, 8th-7th c.BC: Hesiodus Epicus “Opera et Dies” 18, etc.; ν. μετά τινος 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 1105 (Lyric poetry): _metaphorically_, τὴν σὴν δ᾽ ὁμοῦ ναίουσαν [ὀργήν] [prev. author] “OT” 338; τὰν ἀρετὰν ναίειν ἐπὶ πέτραις 4th-5th c.BC: Simonides Lyricus 58]]: with adverb, [κακότης] ἐγγύθι ναίει [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th-7th c.BC: Hesiodus Epicus “Opera et Dies” 288; ἵνα αἱ Φορκίδες ναίουσι 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Prometheus Vinctus” 794]]. b. with accusative loci, dwell in, inhabit, οἰκία, δώματα, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 20.288, 8th-7th c.BC: Hesiodus Epicus “Opera et Dies” 8, compare 5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “P.” 7.5, +others]]; ἅλα, πλάκας ὀρέων, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Helena” 1584, “Ba.” 719; frequently with place-names, 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 2.615, 2nd c.AD: Alexander Rhetor 22, etc.: _metaphorically_, Πειθὼ ναίει καὶ Χάρις υἱὸν Ἄγησίλα uncertain in 5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “Fragmenta.” 123.10]]; of the statues of gods, πρόπυλα ναίουσιν τάδε [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Electra” 1375]]:—passive, to be inhabited, [Refs [[prev. author] “fragment” 1125 (in _aorist_ ἐνάσθη), etc.]]; πολίταις [Refs 3rd c.BC+ [3rd c.BC: Theocritus Poeta Bucolicus 16.88; ὑπ᾽ ἀνδράσι 3rd c.BC: Apollonius Rhodius Epicus 1.794.]]

__2
of places, lie, be situated, once in [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus, νήσων αἳ ναίουσι πέρην ἁλός 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 2.626; ὦ κλεινὰ Σαλαμίς, σὺ μέν που ναίεις ἁλίπλακτος 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Ajax” 598 (Lyric poetry).]]

__II
causal, in Epic dialect aorist ἔνασσα or νάσσα, middle ἐνασσάμην:

__II.1
with accusative loci, give one to dwell in, καί κέ οἱ Ἄργεϊ νάσσα πόλιν I would have given him a town in Argos for his home, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 4.174]]; make habitable, build, νηὸν ἔνασσαν [Refs [“hymnus ad Apollinem” 298]]; settle, Εὔβοιαν ἕλον καὶ ἔνασσαν [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “Pae.” 5.36]]:—in middle, found, μυρία δ᾽ ἄστη νάσσατ᾽ ἐποιχόμενος [Refs 3rd c.BC+ [3rd c.BC: Apollonius Rhodius Epicus 4.275:]] —in passive, of places, like active [Refs [1.2]], to be situated, πολίων εὖ ναιομενάων [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 3.400, +others]]

__II.2
with accusative person, let one dwell, settle him, ἐν Ἄργει ἔνασσεν Ἡρακλέος ἐκγόνους [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “P.” 5.71]]:— in middle, νάσσατο κούρην [Refs 3rd c.BC+ [3rd c.BC: Apollonius Rhodius Epicus 4.567.]]

__III

9. Mid., of cattle, to feed , i. e. go to pasture, graze , Lat. pasci, (Homer), etc.: with accusative cognate to feed on , (Herdotus Historicus), etc.; of men, to eat , (Sophocles Tragicus); of fire, to consume, devour , (Iliad by Homer), etc.; of cancerous sores, to spread , ἐνέμετο πρόσω (Herdotus Historicus)

__I

__II.2
of things, to be gone, lost, vanished, πῇ δή τοι μένος οἴχετα; whither is thy spirit gone? deep_entry:
Abbott-Smith / STEPBible (TBESG)
1. a large bird, bird of prey , such as a vulture  or eagle , and so distinguished from a common bird  ὄρνις); (Homer), etc.
2. a bird of omen  or augury , (Homer), etc.:—;the flight to  (not from)  the right, i. e. towards the East, was fortunate, and vice versa.
3. an omen, presage , drawn from these birds, Lat. auspicium or augurium , according as taken from seeing their flight  or hearing their cry , (Iliad by Homer), etc.; δέκομαι τὸν οἰωνόν I accept the omen , hail it as favourable, (Herdotus Historicus)
commonly derivation from οἶος, —; most birds of prey being solitary, —;  compare κοινωνός from κοινός (ML)

οἰωνός, ὁ,
a large bird, bird of prey, οἰωνοί, φῆναι ἢ αἰγυπιοὶ γαμψώνυχες [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 16.216]]; of the eagle, Κρονίωνι.. φίλτατος οἰωνῶν [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 24.293]]; called οἰωνῶν βασιλεύς by [Refs 5th c.BC+ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Agamemnon” 114 (Lyric poetry), 5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “O.” 13.21, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Aves” 515; ἀρχὸς οἰ. 5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “P.” 1.14]]; mentioned as devouring carcasses, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.5, 22.335, compare 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Antigone” 205, 698, “Aj.” 830; οἰωνοὶ ὠμησταί 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 11.453; θῆρές τ᾽ οἰωνοί τε 5th c.BC: Empedocles Poeta Philosophus 21.11, 130.2]]; ὑπ᾽ οἰωνῶν ταφέντα, of corpses devoured by carrion birds, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Septem contra Thebas” 1025, compare 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Antigone” 29]]; as an image of swiftness, οἰωνοῖς ἅμ᾽ ἕπονται [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th-7th c.BC: Hesiodus Epicus “Theogonia” 268.]]

__2
generally, birds, opposed to beasts, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Fragmenta” 941.11]]; so in οἰωνοκτόνος.

__II
a bird of omen or augury, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 12.237, 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 15.532, 8th-7th c.BC: Hesiodus Epicus “Opera et Dies” 801; τοὺς ἄνωθεν φρονιμωτάτους οἰωνούς 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Electra” 1059 (Lyric poetry); οὔτ᾽ ἀπ᾽ οἰωνῶν.., οὔτ᾽ ἐκ θεῶν του γνωτόν [prev. author] “OT” 395, compare 398; οἰ. αἴσιοι 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 3.3.22, compare 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 12.237, 1st-2nd c.AD: Plutarchus Biographus et Philosophus 2.282d]]; of augurs, καθέζεσθαι ἐπ᾽ οἰωνῶν, ἐπ᾽ οἰωνοῖς καθῆσθαι, [Refs [[prev. author] “Rom.” 22, “Caes.” 47]]; οἱ ἐπ᾽ οἰωνοῖς ἱερεῖς the augurs, [Refs [[prev. author] “Ant.” 5.]]

__III
omen, token, presage, drawn from these birds, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 2.859, +others, compare 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Hippolytus” 873]]; εἷς οἰ. ἄριστος ἀμύνεσθαι περὶ πάτρης the one best omen is to fight for fatherland, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 12.243]]; οἰ. ἀγαθοί good omens, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th-7th c.BC: Hesiodus Epicus “Fragmenta” 134.11]]; δέκομαι τὸν οἰ. I accept the omen, hail it as auspicious, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 9.91; οὗτος οἰ. μέγας 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Orestes” 788; δέδοικα.. τὸν οἰ. 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Equites” 28; τοῦ ἔκπλου οἰ. ἐδόκει εἶναι 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 6.27]]; οἰωνὸν θέσθαι or τίθεσθαι take as an omen, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Phoenissae” 858, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus Alcaeus2.151b; εἰς οἰ. τίθεσθαι χρηστόν 1st-2nd c.AD: Plutarchus Biographus et Philosophus “Lucullus” 36; πρὸς οἰωνοῦ τ. 2nd c.AD: Athenaeus Epigrammaticus 1.13e; οἰωνόν τινα ποιεῖσθαι 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Leges” 702c]]; δι᾽ οἰωνοῦ λαμβάνειν, πρὸς οἰωνοῦ λαβεῖν, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [1st c.BC: Dionysius Halicarnassensis 2.67, 3.13; οἰωνοῦ χάριν 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Menexenus” 249b.]]

__II
referring to a definite object, properly only when a general notion is implied, Πολυκράτεα.., δι᾽ ὅντινα κακῶς ἤκουσε, not the man through whom, but one through whom.., [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 3.120]]; τελευταῖόν σε προσβλέψαιμι νῦν, ὅστις πέφασμαι φύς τ᾽ ἀφ᾽ ὧν οὐ χρῆν may I see thee now for the last time, I who am one born from sinful parentage, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Tyrannus” 1184, compare 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Prometheus Vinctus” 38, “Ag.” 1065]]; but in quite definite sense, βωμόν, ὅστις νῦν ἔξω τῆς πόλεώς ἐστι [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 6.3: sometimes even with οὗτος or ὅδε as antecedent, 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.167, 2.99, 6.47, 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Hippolytus” 943, 3rd c.BC: Theocritus Poeta Bucolicus 8.87.]]

__II.2
ἐφ᾽ ὅτῳ, ={ἐφ᾽ ᾧτε}, [Refs 2nd c.BC+ [1st c.BC: Diodorus Siculus Historicus 16.4; so ἐφ᾽ ὅτῳ τε “Delph.” 3(2).236 (2nd c.BC).]]

__III
in indirect questions, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus, etc., εἴπ᾽ ἄγε μοι καὶ τόνδε.., ὅς τις ὅδ᾽ ἐστί 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 3.192, compare 167, etc.]]; ἔσπετε νῦν μοι, Μοῦσαι, ὅς τις δὴ κτλ. who it was that..,[Refs 8th c.BC+ [14.509; ξεῖνος ὅδ᾽, οὐκ οἶδ᾽ ὅς τις 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 8.28: in dialogue, when the person questioned repeats the question asked by τίς, as οὗτος τί ποιεῖ;—ὅ τι ποι; 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Ranae” 198]]; ἀλλὰ τίς γὰρ ε;—ὅστις; πολίτης χρηστός [Refs 5th c.BC+ [[prev. author] “Ach.” 595, compare “Pl.” 462, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Euthyphro” 2c, etc.]]

__III.2
rare and late in direct questions, ὅ τι ἐστὶ τὸ ἐμποδίζον ; [Refs 2nd c.AD+ [2nd c.AD: Apollonius Dyscolus Grammaticus “de Adverbiis;” 140.12]]; ἀνθ᾽ ὅτου.. ; = why? [Refs 4th c.AD+ [4th c.AD: Julianus Imperator “Epistulae” 82p.109B.]]-C.; compare ὅπως.

__IV
limited or made more indefinite by the addition of Particles:

__IV.1

Related to:  οὐδέ,
negative Particle, related to μηδέ as οὐ to μή, partly conjunction, partly adverb:

__A
CONJUNCTION, but not, mostly answering to μέν (sometimes written divisim), [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 5.138, 24.418; without μέν, 5.21, etc.: sometimes the first οὐδέ]], but not, is followed by οὐδέ, nor, ἄλλοις μὲν πᾶσιν ἑήνδανεν, οὐδέ ποθ᾽ Ἥρῃ, οὐδὲ Ποσειδάων᾽, οὐδὲ γλαυκώπιδι κούρῃ [Refs [24.25.]]

__A.II
more frequently and not, nor: sometimes without a negative preceding, Κίρκη δ᾽ ὡς ἐνόησεν ἔμ᾽ ἥμενον, οὐδ᾽ ἐπὶ σίτῳ χεῖρας ἰάλλοντα [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 10.375; τραχὺς μόναρχος οὐδ᾽ ὑπεύθυνος 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Prometheus Vinctus” 326, compare 102, 259, +others]]; δεινὸν γάρ, οὐδὲ ῥητόν [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 756, compare 996, “OT” 398, 868 (Lyric poetry), 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.97, etc.]]: after a negative compound, ὃν ἠτίμησ᾽ Ἀγαμέμνων, οὐδ᾽ ἀπέλυσε θύγατρα [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.95; ἀνήμεροι γὰρ οὐδὲ πρόσπλατοι ξένοις 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Prometheus Vinctus” 716; ἄστιπτος οὐδ᾽ οἰκουμένη 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 2; ἄθικτος οὐδ᾽ οἰκητός [prev. author] “OC” 39.]]

__A.II.2
with a negative preceding, nor, βρώμης δ᾽ οὐχ ἅπτεαι οὐ. ποτῆτος [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 10.379; οὐκέτισοὶ.. μένος ἔμπεδον οὐ. τις ἀλκή 22.226; οὐκ ἔχων βάσιν οὐ. τιν᾽ ἐγχώρων 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 692 (Lyric poetry), compare 681 (Lyric poetry), 905, 955, 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Oeconomicus” 20.2, etc.: sometimes the preceding _negative_ is itself οὐδέ]], = and not, as in [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 22.222]]; οὐδέ, = nor may be repeated any number of times, e.g. three times in [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Tyrannus” 1378.]] —Sts. the _negative_ follows the whole word-group instead of preceding it, σιδήρῳ δὲ οὐδ᾽ ἀργύρῳ χρέωνται οὐδέν but iron or silver use they not at all, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.215; Θεσσαλοῦ μὲν οὐδ᾽ Ἱππάρχου οὐδεὶς παῖς 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 6.55; ἁπλοῦν μὲν οὐ. δίκαιον οὐδὲν ἂν εἰπεῖν ἔχοι 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 22.4: but οὐδὲ.. οὐδέ]] never means neither.. nor (like οὔτε.. οὔτε); where this combination occurs, the first οὐδέ is used without reference to the second, e.g. καὶ μὴν οὐδ᾽ ἡ ἐπιτείχισις οὐδὲ τὸ ναυτικὸν ἄξιον φοβηθῆναι and moreover we have no reason to fear their fortifications, nor yet their navy, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.142.]]

__A.III
οὐδέ may also follow οὔτε, by an anacoluthon, as in τε.., δέ.. (see. οὔτε [Refs [11.3)]]; but οὔτε cannot follow οὐδέ.[Refs 4th c.BC+ [Cf. — μηδέ 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus 2.]]

__B
adverb, not even, in [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus mostly with _adverbs_, οὐδ᾽ ῃβαιόν]] not even a little, no not a bit, not at all, [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 2.386; οὐ. τυτθόν 1.354; οὐ. μίνυνθα 20.27]]; so also ἐπεὶ οὔ οἱ ἔνι φρένες οὐδ᾽ ἠβαιαί he has no sense, no not even a little,[Refs 8th c.BC+ [14.141, compare 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 21.288; τότε μὲν εὖ ζῶντες, νῦν δὲ οὐ. ζῶντες 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 329a: frequently in _Attic dialect_, τούτῳ μὲν οὐ. διελέγετο]] he did not even exchange words with him, [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Lysias Orator 3.31, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Nubes” 425; οὐδ᾽, εἰ γέγονεν, οἶδα 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 18.70, etc.]]: in the same sense, οὐ. γ᾽ [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedo” 97a, 97b, 106b; οὐ. γ᾽ αὖ [prev. author] “R.” 499a; οὐ. μήν 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 3.3.50, etc.]]; Epic dialect οὐ. μέν [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 9.374, etc.: in _Attic dialect_ frequently with εἷς (whence οὐδείς), οὐδ᾽ ἂν εἷς θύσειεν 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Plutus” 137: sometimes without elision, οὐδὲ εἷς [prev. work] 1182, 3rd c.BC: Herodas Mimographus 1.45; οὐκ ἄλλ᾽ οὐ. ἕν 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Plutus” 138, compare “Ra.” 927; also οὐ. καθ᾽ ἕν 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 2.87; οὐ. παρ᾽ ἑνός 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 2.3.10, etc.]] —This οὐδέ frequently follows καί, and not even, καὶ οὐδ᾽ αὐτοὶ αὖ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ.. [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 7.56, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 3.2.4, etc.]]; also ἀλλ᾽ οὐδέ, most frequently in phrase ἀλλ᾽ οὐδ᾽ ὧς.. [Refs 8th c.BC+ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 7.263, 9.351, etc.]]

__B.II
also not, not.. either, nor yet.., ὁ δίκαιος τοῦ δικαίου δοκεῖ τί σοι ἂν ἐθέλειν πλέον ἔχειν; Answ. οὐδαμῶς..; Qu. τί δ; τῆς δικαίας πράξεως; Answ. οὐ. τῆς δικαίας [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 349b, compare “Ap.” 19d, 21d, 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Memorabilia” 3.11.4.]]

__C

in Relat. as well as antecedent clause, ὥσπερ οὐδ᾽ ηὔχετο, οὐδ᾽ ᾤετο [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus Alcaeus2.141a, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 1.6.18.]]

οὐ γὰρ οὐδέ, as ἀλλ᾽ οὐ γὰρ οὐ. νουθετεῖν ἔξεστί σε [Refs 5th c.BC+ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Electra” 595, compare “Aj.” 1242, “OT” 287, etc.]]; οὐ. γὰρ οὐ. short_definition: on foot — 1. on foot , πεζοί fighters on foot , opposite to horsemen, (Homer):—;also on land, going by land , opposite to sea-faring, (Homer):—;so, ὁ πεζὸς στρατός, or ὁ πεζός alone, sometim
deep_entry:
Abbott-Smith / STEPBible (TBESG)
1. on foot , πεζοί fighters on foot , opposite to horsemen, (Homer):—;also on land, going by land , opposite to sea-faring, (Homer):—;so, ὁ πεζὸς στρατός, or ὁ πεζός alone, sometimes foot-soldiery, infantry , opposite to cavalry  ἡ ἵππος); (Herdotus Historicus)
2. ὁ πεζός, also, a land-force  or army , opposite to a naval force, (Herdotus Historicus); so, τὸ πεζόν (Herdotus Historicus); στρατιὰ καὶ ναυτικὴ καὶ πεζή (Thucydides); τὰ πεζὰ κράτιστοι strongest by land , (Thucydides)
3. of animals, land , as opposite to birds and fishes, τὰ π. καὶ τὰ πτηνά beasts  and birds, (Plato Philosophus)
4. metaphorically of language, not rising above the ground, prosaic , (Lucian)
5. dative feminine πεζῇ (entry ὁδῷ); as adverb, on foot , (Xenophon Historicus)
6. by land , (Thucydides) (ML)

deep_entry:

1. to soften, ripen  or change , by means of heat:
2. of the sun, to ripen  fruit, (Odyssey by Homer); compare πεπαίνω.

deep_entry:
Abbott-Smith / STEPBible (TBESG)
1. neuter πῖον, genitive πίονος, fat, plump , Lat. pinguis, (Homer); π. δημός rich  fat, (Iliad by Homer); of oil, (Herdotus Historicus)
2. of soil, fat, rich.  (Iliad by Homer); also, πίονα ἔργα pingues segetes , (Iliad by Homer); ὀπώρας πίων ποτός, of wine, (Sophocles Tragicus)
3. of persons and places, rich, wealthy , (Homer); πίονι μέτρῳ in plenteous  measure, (Theocritus Poeta Bucolicus)
4. The comparative and Sup. are πι-ότερος, πι-ότατος, as if from πῖος. (ML)

short_definition: sideways — 1. placed sideways, slanting, aslant , Lat. obliquus, (Thucydides)
deep_entry:
Abbott-Smith / STEPBible (TBESG)
1. placed sideways, slanting, aslant , Lat. obliquus, (Thucydides)
2. πλάγια, ων, τά, the sides , (Herdotus Historicus):—;in military sense, τοῖς πλαγίοις ἐπιέναι to attack the flanks , (Thucydides); εἰς τὰ πλ. παράγειν or παραπέμπειν to make an army file off right and left , (Xenophon Historicus); πλαγίους λαβεῖν τοὺς πολεμίους to take the enemy in flank , (Xenophon Historicus)
3. with Preps. in adverbial sense, εἰς πλάγιον obliquely , (Xenophon Historicus); εἰς τὰ πλάγια, opposite to εἰς τὸ ἀντίον, (Thucydides); ἐκ πλαγίου in flank , (Thucydides); κατὰ πλάγια (Xenophon Historicus)
4. metaphorically not straightforward, crooked, treacherous , φρένες (Pindar); πλάγια φρονεῖν (Euripides) (ML)

deep_entry:
Abbott-Smith / STEPBible (TBESG)
1. in early Greek only as Dep.
2. absolute to work hard, do work, suffer toil , (Homer); περὶ δόρπα πονέοντο were busied  about their supper, (Iliad by Homer); so, πεπόνητο καθ᾽ ἵππους was busy  with the horses, of a charioteer, (Iliad by Homer)
3. metaphorically to be in distress, to distress oneself , (Iliad by Homer):—; to suffer, be sick , (Thucydides)
4. with accusative to work hard at, to make  or do with pains  or care , (Homer)
5. after (Homer), the active form prevails
6. intransitive to toil, labour , (Theognis Elegiacus), attic; μάτην π. to labour  in vain, (Sophocles Tragicus); with accusative, τὰ μηδὲν ὠφελοῦντα μὴ πόνει do  not labour at things that profit not, (Aeschulus Tragicus)
7. with accusative cognate, π. πόνον, μόχθους to go through, suffer  them, [variant datesTragica Adespota; also with accusative partis, πονεῖν τὰ σκέλη (Aristophanes Comicus)
8. absolute to labour, be hard-pressed, suffer , (Thucydides): to be worn out, spoilt , (Demosthenes Orator)
9. Pass., impersonal, οὐκ ἄλλως αὐτοῖς πεπόνηται = πεπονήκασι, (Plato Philosophus)
10. transitive,
11. with accusative pers. to afflict, distress , (Pindar):—;Pass. to be worn out, to suffer greatly , (Sophocles Tragicus)
12. Pass., also, to be trained  or educated , (Aristotle Philosopher)
13. with accusative rei, like ἐκπονεῖν, to gain by toil  or labour , χρήματα (Xenophon Historicus): Pass. to be won  or achieved by toil , (Pindar) (ML)
